einzeiler: A space architect and a philosopher discuss human thriving, space exploration and…
kurzfassung: Ariel Ekblaw and Meghan Sullivan explore what enables human flourishing by connecting space architecture with moral philosophy. They discuss how aiming for ambitious goals like space exploration can drive solutions for problems on Earth. Additionally, they examine the role of human-level institutions and attention in building a better society.
stichpunkte: Experiencing Earth from low-Earth orbit often moves even highly trained astronauts to tears.
Artificial intelligence carries the potential to help people realize what it means to be genuinely human.
Human thriving requires high intensity and active attention, unlike animals that mature instinctively.
Space exploration yields tangible benefits for Earth, such as biological research for medical cures.
Ambitious goals like lunar missions motivate people to solve complex problems.
National service programs could unite diverse groups of young people and build community trust.
Institutions like education, religious organizations, and media shape human outlook and purpose.

clips.text: Even exceptionally brave and well-prepared military astronauts are moved to tears when viewing the planet from orbit.

clips.hook: Why squirrels have it easier than humans
clips.text: While animals naturally mature into their capabilities with minimal effort, humans must invest substantial work to develop properly.
Orbital conditions alter biological processes in ways that could potentially accelerate research into cancer treatments, Alzheimer's disease, and organoids.
Implementing a universal year of service for young adults could successfully bridge divides between rural, urban, red, and blue communities.
Because humans function as social creatures, community-level organizations require renewed investment and active participation.

beschreibung:
Philosopher Meghan Sullivan and space architect Ariel Ekblaw don't usually work at the same altitude ... but put them in a room together, and they'll answer the big questions. Drawing on wisdom from Aristotle to astronauts, they discuss what humans inherently owe each other, what it takes to live a good life and what a rulebook for a better world might look like. (This conversation is part of “TED Intersections,” a series featuring thought-provoking conversations between experts navigating the ideas shaping our world.)
